title: Capacitors and dielectrics: charge, voltage and energy
voiceInstructions: Warm, engaging female teacher with a natural General American English accent. Relaxed, welcoming and lightly playful, with a gentle smile and conversational rhythm. Keep scientific terms precise and avoid an announcer cadence. Slow down for equations, numbers and conversions. Give brief natural thinking pauses after questions. Do not add words or laughter absent from the script.

sources.title: NTA: Official JEE Main 2026 syllabus, Physics Unit 11
OpenStax: Energy stored in a capacitor

chapters.title: Capacitance belongs to the arrangement
chapters.formula: C = Q/V; Q is one plate's charge magnitude; 1 F = 1 C/V
points: A simple capacitor has equal opposite plate charges, not net charge 2Q.
For an ideal linear capacitor, geometry and dielectric determine capacitance.
Voltage and charge change together when capacitance is unchanged.
chapters.script: Hey, welcome back. A capacitor separates charge between conductors. In our simple two-plate model, one plate carries plus Q and the other minus Q. The pair can have zero net charge while still storing electrical energy. When we say the charge on the capacitor is Q, we mean the magnitude on one plate, not twice that magnitude. Capacitance is charge magnitude divided by the potential difference magnitude between the conductors. One farad means one coulomb per volt. It tells us how much separated charge this arrangement holds for a given voltage. For an ideal linear capacitor with fixed geometry and material, capacitance doesn't increase just because we apply a higher voltage. Charge increases in the same ratio. If capacitance is three microfarads and voltage is four volts, each plate carries twelve microcoulombs in magnitude. Double voltage to eight volts and charge becomes twenty four microcoulombs, while capacitance remains three microfarads. A microfarad is one millionth of a farad, whereas a picofarad is one trillionth. Keep those prefixes straight. In electrostatic equilibrium the conducting plates are each equipotential, and field within their conducting material is zero. The insulating gap can still have a field. Real capacitors have leakage and voltage limits, so this ideal linear model has a range of validity. For JEE, first identify the two conductors, the voltage between them and what Q represents before applying the ratio.

chapters.title: Parallel plates: geometry controls capacitance
chapters.formula: C0 = epsilon0 A/d; E approximately V/d; assume negligible edge effects
points: Larger plate area increases capacitance; greater separation reduces it.
The standard formula assumes a small gap compared with plate dimensions.
A fully filling uniform linear dielectric gives C = kappa epsilon0 A/d.
chapters.script: Let's derive the parallel-plate result rather than treating it as magic. Take large opposite plates with charge magnitudes Q, area A and separation d, with vacuum in the gap. Well away from the edges, the combined field is approximately Q divided by epsilon zero times area. Potential difference magnitude is field times separation. Divide Q by that potential difference, and capacitance becomes epsilon zero times area divided by separation. Charge cancels, because the geometry sets the ratio. Bigger plates spread a given charge over more area and reduce the voltage needed to hold it. Bringing plates closer also lowers that voltage, increasing capacitance. Use area zero point zero two square meters and separation one millimeter. With epsilon zero equal to eight point eight five times ten to the minus twelve, capacitance is one hundred and seventy seven picofarads. At twelve volts the gap field is twelve thousand newtons per coulomb. This model ignores edge fringing and assumes the gap is small relative to plate dimensions. If a uniform linear dielectric completely fills the gap, multiply the vacuum capacitance by its relative permittivity, kappa. Partial filling requires a different geometry calculation; don't apply that multiplier to the entire capacitor automatically. Also, changing separation has different consequences depending on whether a battery maintains voltage or whether the disconnected plates retain their charge. We'll use that fixed-quantity reasoning throughout the rest of this class.

chapters.title: Series and parallel: follow the nodes
points: Parallel capacitors share the same two nodes and therefore the same voltage.
A simple initially uncharged series chain has equal charge magnitudes and additive voltage drops.
For series capacitors, the smaller capacitance gets the larger voltage drop.
chapters.script: In a network, identify connected nodes rather than relying on how close symbols look on the page. Capacitors are in parallel when both connect across the same two nodes. They share voltage, so total separated charge is the sum of each capacitance times that voltage. Equivalent capacitance is the sum. Two and three microfarads in parallel across ten volts give five microfarads overall, with charges twenty and thirty microcoulombs. Now connect the two capacitors in a simple series chain that starts uncharged, with an isolated neutral intermediate node. The plate charge magnitudes are equal. Their voltage drops add, so the reciprocal of equivalent capacitance is the sum of the individual reciprocals. Two and three microfarads in series give one point two microfarads. Across ten volts, each capacitor carries twelve microcoulombs in magnitude. Their voltages are six volts across the two microfarad capacitor and four volts across the three microfarad capacitor. The smaller capacitance gets the larger voltage, because voltage equals the common charge divided by capacitance. Pause and check: six plus four returns the applied ten volts. Series equivalent capacitance is smaller than either component; parallel equivalent is larger than either. If an internal node already has net charge or another connection, the simple equal-charge assumption may fail. For more complicated JEE networks, label nodes, simplify valid series or parallel groups, and then work backward to recover individual charges and voltages.

chapters.title: Stored energy: choose the right form
chapters.formula: U = Q^2/(2C) = CV^2/2 = QV/2; vacuum field energy density = epsilon0 E^2/2
points: Charging work grows as the capacitor voltage rises, giving the factor one-half.
Use Q squared over 2C when charge is fixed; use CV squared over 2 when voltage is fixed.
Include batteries and mechanical work in the energy balance when geometry changes.
chapters.script: Why is stored energy one half Q V instead of Q V? While charging an initially uncharged ideal capacitor, the voltage rises from zero to its final value. Each small added charge needs work equal to the voltage at that moment times the added charge. Integrating those contributions gives Q squared divided by twice capacitance. Substitute Q equals C V to get one half C V squared, or one half Q V. These are equivalent expressions, not three different kinds of energy. For two microfarads at ten volts, stored energy is one hundred microjoules and charge is twenty microcoulombs. If this capacitor stays disconnected with no leakage and its plate separation doubles, capacitance halves. Charge stays fixed, so energy doubles and voltage doubles. An external agent must do work to pull the attracting plates apart. If instead an ideal battery holds the voltage at ten volts while separation doubles, capacitance halves, plate charge halves and stored energy halves. In that case charge flows back toward the source, and the source belongs in the energy account. Don't infer mechanical work from the capacitor energy change alone. In vacuum, the field energy per unit volume is one half epsilon zero times field squared. For the ideal parallel-plate geometry, multiplying by the gap volume reproduces the capacitor energy. Your formula choice should follow the constraint, not whichever expression looks shortest.

chapters.title: Dielectric insertion: connected or disconnected?
chapters.formula: Cnew = kappa C0; isolated: Q fixed, Vnew = V0/kappa, Unew = U0/kappa; battery: V fixed, Qnew = kappa Q0, Unew = kappa U0
points: Polarization produces bound charges, not free conduction through an ideal dielectric.
Disconnected plates retain charge; connected plates can exchange charge with the battery.
The capacitance multiplier assumes the dielectric completely fills the gap.
chapters.script: A dielectric is an insulating material whose charges respond to the electric field through polarization. Opposite bound charges appear near its faces. They are not the same as freely conducting charges moving across the gap. With fixed free plate charge, polarization reduces the gap field and voltage, so the ratio Q over V increases. Let's completely fill a capacitor's gap with a uniform linear dielectric of kappa three, keeping plate geometry unchanged. Start with two microfarads at ten volts: charge twenty microcoulombs and energy one hundred microjoules. Disconnect the battery first, assuming no leakage. Capacitance becomes six microfarads, charge remains twenty microcoulombs, voltage becomes about three point three three volts, and energy becomes about thirty three point three microjoules. The energy reduction is available for mechanical work and any losses; it has not vanished. Now repeat from the same initial state but keep the ideal ten volt battery connected. Capacitance still becomes six microfarads, but voltage stays ten volts. Charge increases to sixty microcoulombs and stored energy to three hundred microjoules. The battery supplies additional energy, so the increased capacitor energy does not contradict attraction pulling the dielectric inward. With fixed gap and fixed voltage, the average gap field stays V over d; the battery's extra free charge compensates for polarization. Real materials also have dielectric breakdown limits. Our final checklist is: state the geometry, name the material model, identify whether Q or V is fixed, then calculate capacitance, charge, voltage and energy consistently.

quiz.question: An ideal 3 microF capacitor is at 4 V. Charge magnitude on either plate is:
quiz.explanation: Q = CV = 3 microF x 4 V = 12 microC; do not add both plate magnitudes.

quiz.question: Vacuum plates have A = 0.02 m squared and d = 0.001 m. With epsilon0 = 8.85 x 10^-12 and negligible fringing, C is:
quiz.explanation: C = epsilon0 A/d = 1.77 x 10^-10 F = 177 pF.

quiz.question: Initially uncharged 2 microF and 3 microF capacitors form a simple series chain across 10 V. Voltage across the 2 microF capacitor is:
quiz.explanation: Ceq = 1.2 microF; common charge is 12 microC. V1 = Q/C1 = 6 V.

quiz.question: A 2 microF capacitor at 10 V stores:
quiz.explanation: U = CV squared/2 = 2 microF x 100/2 = 100 microJ.

quiz.question: A 2 microF capacitor charged to 10 V is disconnected. A kappa = 3 dielectric completely fills its gap. Final voltage is approximately:
quiz.explanation: Charge stays fixed; capacitance triples, so voltage becomes 10/3 V.

quiz.question: Starting instead with the same capacitor still connected to an ideal 10 V battery, fully inserting kappa = 3 makes stored energy:
quiz.explanation: Voltage stays fixed and capacitance triples. U = CV squared/2 therefore triples to 300 microJ.
